title: Using RL Agent to Detect and Remediate ETL Pipeline Failures - Anna Marie Benzon
talk_summary: Anna Marie Benzon describes an RL-guided (tabular Q-learning) decision layer that picks one bounded remediation action for ETL job failures, wrapped by deterministic feature extraction and an external safety-override layer that can escalate or veto. The measured win comes mostly from structured state, bounded actions, and safety constraints rather than RL itself; RL matched a hand-defined policy and beat random selection.

takeaways.technique: Deterministic facts layer + bounded action set + separate safety override
takeaways.what_they_do: They split the system into three concerns: deterministic rules extract observable facts (schema drift, type change, error class, risk score), a small policy selects one action from a fixed set (retry, rollback, quarantine, escalate, log), and a safety layer outside the policy can override passive choices into escalation for critical/unknown cases.

takeaways.technique: Escalation as a first-class action, not a failure
takeaways.what_they_do: They include 'escalate' in the action space and explicitly do not optimize for non-escalation; the safety layer intentionally escalates more when autonomy would be inappropriate.
takeaways.numbers: Safety override reduced non-escalation by ~15.03 points (intentional)

takeaways.technique: Repeated-seed evaluation against a simple baseline
takeaways.what_they_do: They ran 30-36 runs with confidence intervals and compared the learned policy against a hand-defined deterministic baseline and a random baseline, reporting the delta rather than a single favorable run.
takeaways.numbers: RL vs deterministic: 0 points difference within 0.19 CI; vs random: +15.63 points; success 74.63% ±1.51

takeaways.technique: Use the simplest reliable component per decision
takeaways.what_they_do: They deliberately keep deterministic rules for directly observable facts and only use learning for the compact contextual decision, noting ML-ready is not the same as ML-required.
The policy receives a small structured state (failure category, risk level, data-quality condition) rather than raw logs, and every decision is directly inspectable.
Every proposal, override, execution result, and validation outcome is retained to an audit record, and the system reports when an action was unavailable rather than pretending it succeeded.
